lesson.title: TCP UDP and connection lifecycle
lesson.why: Choosing a transport changes which reliability duties belong to the application. A successful TCP connection does not prove a business operation completed, and UDP delivery cannot be assumed merely because sending succeeded.
lesson.what: TCP provides an ordered byte stream with congestion and flow control. UDP provides datagrams without built-in delivery, ordering or retransmission guarantees. Applications add framing, deadlines and any missing reliability semantics.

concepts.name: Connection establishment
concepts.body: TCP normally exchanges SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK before application traffic. Sequence numbers track byte positions. A listener must exist at the destination, but a completed handshake says nothing about database health or application authorization.

concepts.name: Stream versus messages
concepts.body: TCP preserves byte order, not application message boundaries. One send can arrive in several reads or several sends in one read. Use lengths, delimiters or a protocol parser rather than expecting one read per request.

concepts.name: Loss and backpressure
concepts.body: TCP retransmits unacknowledged data and adjusts sending under congestion. Its receive window limits data in flight toward the receiver. UDP applications must decide whether loss, duplication or reordering is acceptable and implement recovery when needed.

concepts.name: Closure and ambiguity
concepts.body: FIN closes one sending direction; peers may close separately. RST aborts a connection. TIME-WAIT helps handle delayed segments and retransmitted closure traffic. Transport delivery acknowledgements still do not prove an application transaction committed.

e2e: Resolve the destination and choose the application transport and port.
Establish TCP state, or send a UDP datagram without a handshake.
Frame application data and handle backpressure, deadlines and delivery uncertainty.
Close gracefully and retain business-operation identifiers for ambiguous outcomes.

tasks.name: Trace the handshake
steps: Draw SYN from client, SYN-ACK from server and ACK from client. Then add an HTTP request. Mark database access after transport setup, explaining why a healthy handshake cannot certify the database.

tasks.name: Parse a byte stream
steps: Offline, receive chunks `HE`, `LLO\nWO`, `RLD\n`. Accumulate until newline: expected messages are HELLO and WORLD, not three chunk-shaped messages. Preserve the incomplete suffix between reads rather than discarding it.

tasks.name: Compare loss semantics
steps: A fictional sensor sends ten UDP datagrams and the receiver observes eight. Calculate 20 percent missing in this sample. Explain why the sender's successful send calls cannot identify which records arrived or guarantee future delivery.

tasks.name: Review a timeout
steps: A TCP connection drops after an order request was transmitted. List two possible outcomes: no commit or committed order with lost response. Recommend an operation identifier and status lookup, not unconditional creation of another order.

key_terms: SYN: TCP connection synchronization flag.
Datagram: bounded UDP message.
Receive window: advertised receiver capacity.
TIME-WAIT: TCP state protecting connection closure.
lesson.safety: Use paper traces only; do not flood sockets, scan destinations or change network settings.
cleanup: Discard synthetic packet traces; no sockets or services remain open.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical TCP client reads half of one JSON document and then two documents together. Is TCP broken?
interview_points: TCP is a byte stream without message boundaries.
Buffer data and use explicit framing.
Preserve incomplete records between reads.
Keep business confirmation separate from transport acknowledgements.

networking/tcp-udp-and-connection-lifecy.core: TCP orders bytes, not messages; UDP preserves datagrams without delivery guarantees. Implement framing, deadlines and business-level recovery. Handshake success and transport acknowledgement are not application success.

storyboard.title: TCP chunks are not application messages
storyboard.objective: Trace framed messages through arbitrary stream reads.

scenes.title: Bytes arrive
scenes.caption: Read boundaries differ from message boundaries.
scenes.narration: The sender transmits two newline-delimited messages, while the receiver obtains arbitrary chunks of their ordered bytes.

scenes.title: Partial record
scenes.caption: Parsing every read as a message fails.
scenes.narration: The first read contains only HE. Treating this chunk as a complete message would discard the remaining characters' context.

scenes.title: Buffer until delimiter
scenes.caption: The parser emits HELLO and WORLD only when complete.
scenes.narration: The receiver preserves incomplete data and emits records at newline boundaries, independent of how many socket reads were required.

lesson.title: DNS resolution caching and troubleshooting
lesson.why: A correct authoritative DNS record can coexist with stale client answers. Understanding caches and delegation helps distinguish normal propagation delay from a broken name, a wrong resolver or an inaccessible application.
lesson.what: DNS maps names to typed records through a hierarchy. A recursive resolver finds answers on a client's behalf and caches them for bounded periods; authoritative servers publish records for zones they control.

concepts.name: Delegation and authority
concepts.body: Resolvers follow referrals from the root toward the authoritative zone when their caches lack an answer. Delegation records and authoritative data have different owners. A correct server record cannot compensate for a broken parent delegation.

concepts.name: Records and aliases
concepts.body: A records contain IPv4 addresses and AAAA records IPv6 addresses. CNAME aliases point to another name, not an IP address or URL path. Applications still select ports and protocols after resolution; DNS success is not service health.

concepts.name: Positive and negative caching
concepts.body: TTL bounds ordinary reuse of cached records, subject to resolver behavior. Negative answers can also be cached using zone information. Lowering a TTL does not retroactively shorten an older answer already cached with a larger lifetime.

concepts.name: Troubleshooting layers
concepts.body: Compare the application's resolver path with recursive and authoritative answers. NXDOMAIN means the name does not exist in that answer context, while other errors indicate different failures. Split-horizon DNS can legitimately return different answers inside and outside a network.

e2e: The client asks its configured resolver for a specific record type.
The resolver checks its cache and follows delegation when necessary.
Authoritative data returns with cache lifetime and the resolver answers the client.
The application connects separately; diagnose stale answers using resolver identity and remaining TTL.

tasks.name: Map resolution roles
steps: Draw a client, recursive resolver and authoritative zone. Label the client-facing answer and the authoritative record owner separately. Explain why editing a workstation hosts file would affect that workstation, not the public authoritative zone.

tasks.name: Calculate remaining TTL
steps: An answer is cached at 12:00 with TTL 300 seconds. At 12:03 its remaining ordinary lifetime is 120 seconds. Changing authoritative TTL to 30 at 12:02 does not force this existing cache to expire at 12:02:30.

tasks.name: Diagnose a negative answer
tasks.goal: Avoid confusing absence with transport failure.
steps: A fictional resolver returns NXDOMAIN after a name was just created. Consider negative caching and the exact queried spelling before changing the application. Compare an authoritative answer with the recursive answer in a paper evidence table.

tasks.name: Plan a DNS migration
tasks.goal: Account for old caches and application checks.
steps: Prepare a fictional endpoint move: lower TTL ahead of the change, wait out the previous TTL, update records and monitor both endpoints. Keep the old endpoint available through the transition and test application responses separately from resolution.

key_terms: Resolver: component obtaining DNS answers.
Authoritative server: publisher for a zone.
TTL: cache lifetime in seconds.
NXDOMAIN: answer indicating a nonexistent name.
lesson.safety: Use fictional names and offline timelines. Do not change real DNS zones or flush shared resolver caches.
cleanup: Retain the migration timeline; no DNS records were created or modified.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical DNS change is visible at the authoritative server but some clients still use the old address. Why?
interview_points: Inspect their resolver path and cached TTL.
Consider prior positive or negative caching.
Check split-horizon views and application caches.
Keep application connectivity diagnosis separate.

networking/dns-resolution-caching-and-tr.core: Follow client → recursive cache → authority. TTL changes affect new answers, not necessarily existing caches. Check negative caching, record type and resolver context before treating different answers as a DNS outage.
objectives: Calculate cache lifetime during a record change.
Distinguish authoritative data from recursive answers.
prerequisites: Know hostnames and IP address families.

storyboard.title: The old DNS answer has not expired
storyboard.objective: Explain stale resolution during a controlled migration.

scenes.title: Cache populated
scenes.caption: The resolver stores an answer with a five-minute TTL.
scenes.narration: The resolver obtains the address and caches it for three hundred seconds, serving later clients from that cached answer.

scenes.title: Authority changes
scenes.caption: The existing cache still has its original lifetime.
scenes.narration: The authoritative address changes, but the resolver's older answer has not expired. A shorter new TTL does not rewrite that cache.

scenes.title: Refresh after expiry
scenes.caption: The resolver retrieves the new authoritative value.
scenes.narration: After expiration, the resolver refreshes the record. The operator also checks application behavior at the new endpoint before retiring the old one.

lesson.title: HTTP HTTPS TLS and certificates
lesson.why: An encrypted connection can still reach the wrong identity if verification is disabled. Separating HTTP semantics from TLS authentication makes status codes, certificate failures and proxy behavior much easier to diagnose.
lesson.what: HTTP defines requests, responses, methods and representations. HTTPS carries HTTP over an authenticated encrypted transport. TLS certificates bind server identity to names through a trusted chain; application authorization remains a separate control.

concepts.name: HTTP semantics
concepts.body: Methods communicate intent: GET retrieves a representation, while POST commonly requests processing with application-defined effects. Status codes report response categories, not universal business success. A 200 response containing an application error still needs interpretation against the API contract.

concepts.name: TLS identity
concepts.body: Clients check the certificate's chain, validity period and requested hostname against its subject alternative names. SNI helps a server choose the appropriate certificate for a hostname. Trusting a certificate is not the same as authorizing the caller.

concepts.name: Termination boundaries
concepts.body: A reverse proxy can terminate TLS and create a new upstream connection. Encryption on the client-to-proxy hop does not prove encryption on the proxy-to-application hop. Record both trust boundaries and forwarded metadata expectations explicitly.

concepts.name: Caching and retries
concepts.body: HTTP caches use freshness and validation rules. Idempotent method semantics support some retries, but application contracts still matter. Retrying a POST after a lost response may duplicate effects unless the service provides an idempotency mechanism.

e2e: Resolve the hostname and establish the transport required by the HTTP version.
Negotiate TLS and verify the server certificate for the requested hostname.
Send the HTTP method, target and headers, then interpret the response contract.
Apply documented caching or retry rules without bypassing authentication failures.

tasks.name: Separate protocol outcomes
steps: Classify three hypothetical results: certificate-name mismatch, HTTP 401 and HTTP 503. Expected layers are server identity verification, application authentication and service availability. Explain why adding an authorization header cannot repair the certificate's wrong hostname.

tasks.name: Calculate certificate timing
steps: A fictional certificate expires October 20 and replacement verification starts October 6. The overlap window is 14 days. Schedule deployment and client-chain checks within that window, not at expiry, and include clock correctness in the diagnosis.

tasks.name: Read a response offline
steps: Review a fictional response: status 200, Content-Type application/json, body containing status=queued. Conclude the request was accepted according to this example contract, not that downstream work finished. Define a separate job-status check for completion.

tasks.name: Map a TLS proxy
steps: Draw browser → TLS proxy → application. Mark the second connection as plain HTTP in the initial design. Describe when that hop crosses an untrusted boundary and propose authenticated upstream TLS without disabling hostname checks or using fabricated certificates.

key_terms: TLS: authenticated encrypted transport protocol.
SAN: certificate field containing permitted identities.
SNI: TLS hostname indication from client.
Termination: endpoint decrypting a TLS connection.
lesson.safety: Use paper protocol examples. Never disable certificate verification or send credentials to test endpoints.
cleanup: Keep only fictional certificate dates and headers; no keys, certificates or network services were created.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical API works only when certificate verification is disabled. How would you diagnose it safely?
interview_points: Check hostname, chain, validity and client clock.
Inspect SNI and proxy termination configuration.
Repair trust or certificate deployment rather than bypassing checks.
Test application authorization only after transport identity succeeds.

networking/http-https-tls-and-certificat.core: HTTPS verifies server identity and encrypts a transport hop; it does not grant application access. Check hostname, chain and validity. Trace proxy-to-backend protection separately and interpret HTTP responses against the API contract.
objectives: Separate TLS failures from HTTP status handling.
Explain certificate verification and proxy termination boundaries.
prerequisites: Understand URLs, hostnames and request-response communication.

storyboard.title: A wrong certificate blocks HTTP before authorization
storyboard.objective: Locate certificate verification in the request path.

scenes.title: Identity before HTTP
scenes.caption: The client verifies the requested hostname.
scenes.narration: The client receives the proxy's certificate and checks its hostname, trust chain and validity before sending an authenticated application request.

scenes.title: Name mismatch
scenes.caption: An authorization token cannot repair server identity.
scenes.narration: The proxy presents a certificate for another name. The client stops before HTTP authorization, so application credentials are not the remedy.

scenes.title: Correct the certificate mapping
scenes.caption: Restore verification instead of bypassing it.
scenes.narration: The operator fixes certificate selection and verifies both transport hops, then checks the API response under the normal authorization policy.

lesson.title: CIDR subnetting routing and NAT
lesson.why: Address planning errors can make a route ambiguous or force costly renumbering later. CIDR arithmetic and packet-path reasoning reveal why address overlap, longest-prefix routing and return paths matter more than familiar subnet labels.
lesson.what: CIDR describes an address block using a prefix length. Routing chooses paths by destination and policy; NAT rewrites addresses or ports and tracks mappings. These functions are related but are not interchangeable security controls.

concepts.name: Prefix arithmetic
concepts.body: An IPv4 prefix leaves 32 minus prefix-length host bits. A /24 contains 256 addresses and a /26 contains 64. Conventional subnet network and broadcast reservations differ from cloud-specific reservations; do not assume every calculated address is assignable.

concepts.name: Longest-prefix matching
concepts.body: A more specific matching destination prefix normally wins over a broader route, subject to policy routing. A /24 route beats a matching /16 even if the latter feels like the main network. The default route matches when no more specific route applies.

concepts.name: NAT mappings
concepts.body: Source NAT replaces the source address, often also translating a port. Return traffic must match the maintained translation. NAT does not authenticate users or encrypt traffic, and translating outbound traffic does not automatically permit arbitrary unsolicited inbound connections.

concepts.name: Overlap and return paths
concepts.body: Two connected networks using the same prefixes can disagree about whether a destination is local or remote. Both directions require viable routing. Asymmetric paths can break stateful inspection or NAT even when one-way packet capture shows successful outbound transmission.

e2e: Determine whether the destination matches a local subnet or routed prefix.
Select the most specific applicable route in the relevant routing context.
Apply any configured address translation and forward toward the next hop.
Ensure the response returns through a valid route and any required translation state.

tasks.name: Divide a subnet
steps: Split 192.0.2.0/24 into four /26 blocks: .0-.63, .64-.127, .128-.191 and .192-.255. Each has 64 total addresses. Identify 192.0.2.70 in the second block; do not treat documentation addresses as deployment instructions.

tasks.name: Choose the winning route
steps: For destination 10.2.3.9 compare routes 0.0.0.0/0, 10.2.0.0/16 and 10.2.3.0/24. The /24 wins in this simple table. Explain why its next hop can still be unhealthy even though route selection is deterministic.

tasks.name: Track a translation
steps: On paper map 10.0.0.5:50000 to documentation address 198.51.100.10:62000 for a TCP connection. Trace the response back through that mapping. Explain why another NAT device without the state cannot necessarily restore the original destination.

tasks.name: Detect overlapping networks
steps: Two fictional sites both use 10.1.0.0/16. Mark the collision before designing their connection. Compare renumbering with carefully managed translation, documenting operational complexity instead of assuming a VPN will resolve conflicting address ownership automatically.

key_terms: CIDR: prefix-based address block notation.
Prefix: leading network-identifying address bits.
NAT: address or port translation.
Default route: fallback route with zero prefix length.
lesson.safety: Use documentation ranges and offline tables only. Do not alter host routes, NAT rules or network interfaces.
cleanup: Retain calculated ranges and remove any real network details from shared diagrams.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical VPN is established but traffic between two sites using the same private subnet fails. Why might that happen?
interview_points: Identify overlapping address ownership.
Inspect both directions and longest-prefix decisions.
Do not confuse tunnel establishment with application reachability.
Prefer a deliberate address plan or controlled translation design.

networking/cidr-subnetting-routing-and-n.core: IPv4 block size is 2^(32-prefix). Select the longest matching route, then inspect return paths and NAT state. NAT rewrites addresses; it does not resolve every overlap or provide authentication and encryption.
objectives: Calculate CIDR blocks and route matches.
prerequisites: Understand IPv4 addresses and binary prefix lengths.

storyboard.title: The most specific route controls the packet
storyboard.objective: Trace routing and source translation separately.

scenes.title: Choose the route
scenes.caption: A matching /24 wins over /16 and default routes.
scenes.narration: The router chooses the most specific destination prefix, then translates the client's source endpoint if the selected path requires NAT.

scenes.title: Return state missing
scenes.caption: A response on another NAT device may not reach the client.
scenes.narration: The reply reaches a device without the original mapping. A correct outbound route alone cannot reconstruct the private destination.

scenes.title: Restore a symmetric stateful path
scenes.caption: Check route selection and translation state in both directions.
scenes.narration: The operator verifies the return route and required mapping, separating address translation from the decision about which next hop to use.

lesson.title: Load balancing proxies and health checks
lesson.why: A load balancer can direct requests only according to the signals it observes. Weak health checks send users to broken backends, while overly broad checks can remove every backend during a shared dependency failure.
lesson.what: Load balancing distributes traffic among eligible targets. Transport-level balancing forwards connections; application proxies interpret protocols such as HTTP. Target readiness, connection lifetime and graceful draining determine what happens during changes or failures.

concepts.name: Layer and routing choice
concepts.body: Layer-four balancing reasons mainly about transport connections. Layer-seven proxies can route by HTTP host or path and terminate TLS. Connection reuse and sticky sessions can make request distribution uneven even when a balancing algorithm appears fair.

concepts.name: Health signal scope
concepts.body: A TCP probe checks acceptance of connections, not correctness of application responses. Readiness should represent whether the target can serve useful traffic. Avoid making every target unhealthy merely because an optional shared dependency is unavailable when degraded service remains possible.

concepts.name: Thresholds and timing
concepts.body: Intervals, timeouts and consecutive-result thresholds trade detection speed against false positives. A single delayed probe need not remove a target. Recovery also needs thresholds; otherwise transient improvement can repeatedly add and remove the same unstable backend.

concepts.name: Draining and retries
concepts.body: Removing a target from new traffic does not instantly finish existing requests. Drain connections within a bounded deadline and account for long-lived sessions. Proxy retries can duplicate unsafe operations unless the request contract supports retry or deduplication.

e2e: A client reaches the balancing frontend and the proxy selects eligible targets.
Health checks update eligibility independently of ordinary request arrivals.
A failed target stops receiving new work while existing work is handled or drained.
Recovery checks restore eligibility after stable readiness, followed by observed user success.

tasks.name: Choose probe depth
tasks.goal: Match a signal to useful service.
steps: A hypothetical API listens on TCP but cannot load its required configuration. Compare TCP acceptance with an application readiness endpoint. Choose a signal that excludes the misconfigured target without querying expensive dependencies on every probe.

tasks.name: Calculate detection timing
steps: Probes occur every ten seconds and require three consecutive failures. If failure begins just before a probe, exclusion is roughly 20 seconds later; just after, roughly 30 seconds, plus probe completion time. Document this range rather than a guaranteed instant.

tasks.name: Plan target draining
steps: Offline, stop new requests to a target at time zero, allow existing requests up to a 30-second deadline and then close remaining connections deliberately. Explain how a two-minute streaming request requires a different rollout contract or reconnect behavior.

tasks.name: Diagnose universal failure
tasks.goal: Avoid amplifying a shared dependency outage.
steps: All targets fail a probe because optional recommendations are unavailable. Propose a degraded response and a readiness check tied to core functionality. Keep a separate alert for recommendation failure rather than hiding it or removing every usable target.

key_terms: Target: backend eligible for traffic.
Readiness: ability to serve useful requests.
Drain: stop new work while finishing existing work.
L7 proxy: intermediary interpreting application protocol data.
lesson.safety: Use fictional probe timelines; do not change production target groups or disable real health checks.
cleanup: Keep the probe contract and discard deployment-specific identifiers; no traffic routing was changed.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical rollout drops long-running requests despite removing old targets before stopping them. What is missing?
interview_points: Separate eligibility from active-connection lifetime.
Configure and observe graceful draining.
Account for streaming and client retry contracts.
Verify readiness before adding replacement targets.

networking/load-balancing-proxies-and-he.core: Health checks define eligibility, not universal correctness. Choose meaningful readiness, bounded detection thresholds and graceful draining. Removing new traffic does not finish active requests, and proxy retries must respect business idempotency.
objectives: Design readiness and draining for a rollout.
prerequisites: Understand HTTP requests and backend replicas.

storyboard.title: Stop new traffic before terminating a target
storyboard.objective: Explain health eligibility and connection draining.

scenes.title: Two eligible targets
scenes.caption: Healthy backends receive traffic.
scenes.narration: The proxy checks readiness and selects eligible backends. Existing connections can continue carrying requests after their initial selection.

scenes.title: Premature termination
scenes.caption: Removal from selection does not complete active requests.
scenes.narration: The old target stops immediately after removal. Its in-flight requests fail because traffic eligibility and connection completion are different states.

scenes.title: Drain deliberately
scenes.caption: Route new work to the replacement and bound old work.
scenes.narration: The rollout sends new requests to the ready replacement and waits for the old target's bounded drain period before termination.

lesson.title: Firewalls security groups and network ACLs
lesson.why: A permitted inbound port does not guarantee a working conversation. Stateful and stateless filters treat return traffic differently, and a broad temporary allow can become a long-lived exposure if rule ownership is unclear.
lesson.what: Packet filters evaluate traffic against source, destination, protocol and port rules. Security groups and network ACLs are provider-specific implementations; understand their state tracking, rule ordering and attachment scope rather than transferring assumptions between platforms.

concepts.name: Stateful filtering
concepts.body: A stateful filter recognizes traffic belonging to an allowed flow and can permit its responses automatically. That behavior depends on the product and connection tracking. It does not mean all traffic in both directions is allowed to every destination.

concepts.name: Stateless filtering
concepts.body: A stateless ACL evaluates packets independently. Return traffic needs its own permitted path, including the client's selected source port when it becomes the response destination. Ordered allow and deny rules can cause a broad earlier match to shadow a later exception.

concepts.name: Attachment and scope
concepts.body: A subnet ACL affects traffic at a different boundary from an interface or instance security group. Host firewalls add another layer. A correct rule attached to the wrong resource has no useful effect on the actual request path.

concepts.name: Least exposure and evidence
concepts.body: Allow only required peers, protocols and ports, with an owner and expiry for temporary exceptions. Flow logs can reveal accepted or rejected traffic but do not prove application authorization. Avoid opening all ports just to distinguish filtering from missing listeners.

e2e: Identify the exact source, destination, protocol and ports for the request.
Trace each filtering boundary and evaluate its rules in the documented order.
Model response packets, including ephemeral ports and any connection-tracking behavior.
Confirm the listener and application response separately, then remove unnecessary exceptions.

tasks.name: Build a flow tuple
steps: Offline, describe TCP from 192.0.2.10:51000 to 198.51.100.20:443. Reverse the endpoints for the response: destination port becomes 51000. Explain why a stateless response rule limited to destination port 443 misses this packet.

tasks.name: Evaluate ordered rules
steps: A fictional ordered ACL has rule 100 deny all TCP, then rule 200 allow TCP 443. Under first-match evaluation the HTTPS packet is denied at 100. Reorder a paper copy narrowly rather than changing any actual firewall.

tasks.name: Compare connection tracking
steps: Contrast AWS security groups, which are stateful, with AWS network ACLs, which are stateless. Mark where an explicit return rule is necessary. State that similarly named controls on other platforms require their own documentation, not assumed equivalence.

tasks.name: Diagnose a false firewall lead
steps: A hypothetical allowed flow reaches a host with no listener on the intended port. Predict that adding a broader allow will not create the listener. Request socket and application evidence, keeping the existing least-privilege boundary intact.

key_terms: Stateful: tracking permitted connection context.
Stateless: evaluating packets independently.
Ephemeral port: temporary client-side port.
Five-tuple: protocol plus source/destination addresses and ports.
lesson.safety: Use documentation addresses and paper policies. Do not scan networks or alter real firewall, security-group or ACL rules.
cleanup: Retain only the minimal fictional rule set; no access exceptions were installed.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical HTTPS request passes an inbound ACL but its response never reaches the client. What would you examine?
interview_points: Reverse the flow tuple and inspect ephemeral destination ports.
Check stateless return rules and their ordering.
Confirm state tracking and rule attachment scopes.
Separate filtering from routing and listener failures.

networking/firewalls-security-groups-and.core: Trace both directions across every attached filter. Stateful controls can recognize responses; stateless ACLs need explicit return paths. Rule order and ephemeral ports matter. An allow rule does not create a listener or grant application access.
objectives: Evaluate stateful and stateless response handling.
Identify shadowed rules and incorrect attachment scope.
prerequisites: Understand TCP ports, addresses and request/response flows.

storyboard.title: The response uses the client's ephemeral port

scenes.title: Inbound request passes
scenes.caption: The rule permits the server's destination port.
scenes.narration: The client sends to port four hundred forty-three and the ACL permits the request to reach the server.

scenes.title: Return packet is denied
scenes.caption: The response destination is not port 443.
scenes.narration: The response targets the client's ephemeral port. A stateless rule allowing only destination port four hundred forty-three does not match.

scenes.title: Model both directions
scenes.caption: Use the reversed tuple and documented rule ordering.
scenes.narration: The operator checks the response tuple and ordered ACL rules, then designs the narrow required return path without opening unrelated traffic.

lesson.title: VPN private connectivity and hybrid networks
lesson.why: A healthy tunnel indicator does not prove a hybrid application works. Routing, overlapping addresses, DNS and packet size can still break communication after encryption has successfully established a protected path.
lesson.what: Hybrid networking connects separate administrative networks through VPNs or private connectivity services. A VPN commonly encrypts traffic over another network; a private circuit changes the path but does not automatically provide application authentication or encryption.

concepts.name: Tunnel and application boundaries
concepts.body: IPsec VPNs negotiate security associations that define protected traffic and cryptographic parameters. Tunnel establishment verifies part of the connection, not every destination route or service policy. Applications still need identity, authorization and appropriate end-to-end protection.

concepts.name: Route exchange
concepts.body: Static routes or dynamic protocols such as BGP tell each side which prefixes are reachable. Route advertisements must be filtered and checked for overlap. An established BGP session can advertise the wrong prefixes or an unusable next hop.

concepts.name: MTU and encapsulation
concepts.body: Tunnel headers reduce payload space within the path's maximum transmission unit. Large packets may require fragmentation or path-MTU adaptation. Small pings succeeding while larger application transfers stall can indicate packet-size problems rather than an authentication failure.

concepts.name: Redundancy and DNS
concepts.body: Independent tunnels and devices reduce single points of failure only if routes actually fail over. Private DNS forwarding must resolve the intended internal names in both directions. Duplicate tunnels on one physical device may still share its failure domain.

e2e: Agree nonoverlapping prefixes, trusted peers and name-resolution requirements.
Establish protected connectivity and exchange only approved routes.
Verify bidirectional reachability, filtering and representative packet sizes.
Exercise a paper failover and confirm applications resolve and reconnect through the surviving path.

tasks.name: Separate guarantees
steps: Draw a private circuit and an IPsec tunnel as separate options. Label routing, encryption and application authorization independently. Explain why a private path alone does not justify sending sensitive application traffic without its required cryptographic protection.

tasks.name: Calculate encapsulation headroom
steps: Assume a 1500-byte path MTU and hypothetical tunnel overhead of 80 bytes. Maximum inner packet size is 1420 bytes before considering any additional encapsulation. State that real overhead varies by protocol and must be measured or documented, not copied from this assumption.

tasks.name: Inspect route intent
steps: A fictional site needs 10.20.0.0/16 but receives only 10.30.0.0/16 through its established routing session. Identify the missing advertisement. Do not treat session-up status as proof of reachability or add an unrestricted default route as a shortcut.

tasks.name: Design a failure rehearsal
steps: On paper, remove tunnel A and trace outbound and return routes through B. Check whether both tunnels share a gateway device and whether DNS forwarding remains reachable. Define application reconnect success, not only tunnel status, as recovery evidence.

key_terms: VPN: protected logical network connection.
BGP: protocol exchanging network reachability.
MTU: maximum packet size on a link or path.
Security association: negotiated IPsec protection context.
lesson.safety: Use offline diagrams only. Do not alter VPN peers, routing advertisements, cryptographic keys or production tunnels.
cleanup: Retain anonymized route and packet-size assumptions; no tunnel or circuit was provisioned.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical hybrid tunnel is up and small probes work, but large transfers stall. What would you investigate?
interview_points: Check effective path MTU and encapsulation overhead.
Verify required ICMP and path-MTU behavior.
Inspect both routing directions and filtering.
Avoid assuming tunnel establishment proves application health.

networking/vpn-private-connectivity-and-.core: Hybrid success needs routes, DNS, filtering and packet-size compatibility in addition to a tunnel. Private connectivity is not automatically encryption. Verify independent failover paths and actual application recovery.
objectives: Explain tunnel status versus end-to-end reachability.
Calculate a hypothetical inner-packet size limit.
prerequisites: Understand CIDR routing and encrypted connections.

storyboard.title: A healthy VPN can still stall large packets
storyboard.objective: Connect tunnel overhead with application transfer failure.

scenes.title: Tunnel established
scenes.caption: Small packets fit through the protected path.
scenes.narration: The gateway negotiates protection and forwards small packets. This verifies basic connectivity but not the largest application transfer size.

scenes.title: Large packet stalls
scenes.caption: Encapsulation consumes part of the path MTU.
scenes.narration: A larger packet exceeds the effective path limit after tunnel headers are added. The application stalls although the tunnel remains established.

scenes.title: Diagnose effective MTU
scenes.caption: Check packet-size behavior without disabling protection.
scenes.narration: The operator checks documented overhead and path-MTU behavior, then validates representative transfers through the intended encrypted route.

lesson.title: IPv6 dual stack and service discovery
lesson.why: A service can work over IPv4 while failing over IPv6 for the same hostname. Dual-stack operation means maintaining two reachable paths, not merely publishing an additional DNS record and assuming applications choose correctly.
lesson.what: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses and a different neighbor-discovery model from IPv4. Dual-stack hosts support both families. Service discovery supplies current endpoints, while clients still need connection selection, timeouts and health-aware behavior.

concepts.name: Address notation and scope
concepts.body: IPv6 writes hexadecimal groups separated by colons, compressing one sequence of zero groups with a double colon. Loopback is ::1. Link-local addresses are scoped to a link and commonly need an interface zone when ambiguity exists.

concepts.name: Subnets and discovery
concepts.body: IPv6 commonly uses /64 LAN subnets, particularly with stateless address autoconfiguration. Neighbor Discovery uses ICMPv6 rather than ARP. Indiscriminately blocking ICMPv6 can break essential functions including neighbor discovery and path-MTU handling.

concepts.name: Dual-stack resolution
concepts.body: DNS A and AAAA records advertise IPv4 and IPv6 endpoints. Clients may race or stagger connection attempts using Happy Eyeballs behavior. Publishing an AAAA record before the IPv6 listener, route and filter path work can create selective latency or failures.

concepts.name: Endpoint lifecycle
concepts.body: Service discovery can use DNS or a registry containing healthy endpoints and metadata. Cache lifetime and deregistration delays affect how long removed instances remain visible. A discovered endpoint is a candidate; clients must still handle stale entries and failed connections.

e2e: The client discovers candidate endpoints and supported address families.
It selects or races connection attempts within bounded timeouts.
The chosen family traverses its own routes, neighbor discovery and filters.
Endpoint changes propagate through discovery caches while clients retire failed connections safely.

tasks.name: Expand an address
steps: Offline, expand 2001:db8::5 to 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0005. Confirm eight groups of sixteen bits, totaling 128. This documentation prefix is for examples; do not assign it to a real service.

tasks.name: Compare address-family paths
steps: Draw A and AAAA answers for one fictional hostname. Mark only the IPv4 listener as present. Predict that some clients succeed while IPv6 attempts fail or delay, depending on fallback behavior; DNS publication alone created no IPv6 listener.

tasks.name: Calculate stale endpoint exposure
steps: An endpoint answer is cached for 60 seconds and its instance is removed after ten. Ordinary cache reuse can reference that endpoint for another 50 seconds. Propose draining and bounded reconnect behavior rather than requiring an impossible instant cache purge.

tasks.name: Review an IPv6 filter
steps: A paper firewall denies all ICMPv6 while allowing TCP 443. Identify the risk to neighbor discovery and path-MTU signaling. Replace the blanket assumption with a documented least-privilege control-message policy without changing actual host rules.

key_terms: AAAA: DNS record containing an IPv6 address.
Dual stack: support for IPv4 and IPv6.
NDP: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Protocol.
Happy Eyeballs: bounded multi-path connection selection strategy.
lesson.safety: Use documentation addresses and offline checks. Do not enable interfaces, publish DNS records or modify ICMPv6 filtering.
cleanup: Remove fictional endpoint mappings from notes if mistaken for live configuration; no networking state was changed.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical site becomes intermittently slow after adding an AAAA record. How would you investigate?
interview_points: Test IPv4 and IPv6 listener, route and filter paths separately.
Inspect client connection fallback timing.
Check ICMPv6 and path-MTU dependencies.
Publish only reachable endpoints and plan cache transitions.

networking/ipv6-dual-stack-and-service-d.core: Dual stack requires working IPv4 and IPv6 paths. AAAA publication does not establish reachability. Preserve necessary ICMPv6 functions, use bounded connection selection and account for stale service-discovery entries.
objectives: Expand IPv6 notation and identify address scope.
prerequisites: Understand DNS A records, listeners and routes.

storyboard.title: An AAAA record advertises an unfinished path

scenes.title: Two candidate addresses
scenes.caption: DNS supplies both address families.
scenes.narration: The client discovers IPv4 and IPv6 candidates. Each requires a working listener, route and permitted transport path.

scenes.title: IPv6 is incomplete
scenes.caption: Clients can wait before reaching the working IPv4 path.
scenes.narration: The AAAA record exists but its listener is missing. IPv6 attempts fail or wait, while IPv4 remains healthy.

scenes.title: Verify both families
scenes.caption: Repair the advertised path and retain bounded fallback.
scenes.narration: The operator checks the IPv6 route, control traffic and listener, then validates connection behavior for both families rather than DNS alone.

lesson.title: CDNs caching and edge delivery
lesson.why: Caching can remove repeated origin work and reduce user latency, but an incorrect cache key can expose one user's response to another. Freshness, variation and invalidation are correctness decisions as well as performance choices.
lesson.what: A content delivery network serves cached responses near clients and forwards misses to an origin. HTTP cache directives, cache keys and validation headers determine what can be reused, for whom and for how long.

concepts.name: Cache keys
concepts.body: A key selects which requests share a stored response, commonly incorporating path and selected headers or query parameters. Ignoring a representation-changing input creates incorrect reuse. Including every irrelevant input fragments the cache and lowers the hit ratio.

concepts.name: Freshness and validation
concepts.body: Cache-Control can define freshness or prohibit shared storage. No-cache permits storage but requires validation before reuse; no-store forbids storage. Validators such as ETag support conditional requests, potentially returning 304 without retransmitting an unchanged representation.

concepts.name: Private data boundaries
concepts.body: Authenticated or personalized responses need deliberate shared-cache policy. Cookies and authorization headers must be considered alongside provider behavior. Public static assets and user-specific account pages should not inherit the same caching rules merely because they share a hostname.

concepts.name: Invalidation and origin load
concepts.body: Versioned asset names make new content a different key while older references remain available. Invalidation removes selected cached entries but may take time. Simultaneous misses can overload the origin, so request collapsing and carefully designed stale serving may improve resilience.

e2e: The edge computes a cache key from the request's configured variation inputs.
A fresh permitted response is returned locally; otherwise the edge contacts the origin.
The origin supplies content and cache policy or validates an existing representation.
The edge stores eligible responses and later refreshes, expires or invalidates them according to policy.

tasks.name: Calculate origin demand
steps: For 1,000 requests per second and a 90 percent hit ratio, expected miss traffic is 100 requests per second, ignoring validation and other effects. If the hit ratio falls to 50 percent, origin demand rises fivefold to 500.

tasks.name: Find a dangerous key
steps: A fictional /profile response varies by user but the cache key contains only the path. Explain how two users could receive the same stored representation. Choose a nonshared policy for sensitive profiles rather than adding actual personal data to the exercise.

tasks.name: Interpret cache directives
steps: Offline, compare no-cache and no-store. Expected decision: the first can be stored but must be validated before reuse; the second must not be stored. Explain why treating their names as interchangeable produces incorrect cache behavior.

tasks.name: Plan an asset release
steps: Use fictional asset names app.a1.js and app.b2.js. Publish the new asset before updating HTML references and retain the old asset for existing clients. Describe HTML freshness separately; deleting the old file immediately can break cached pages.

key_terms: Hit ratio: fraction served from cache.
Origin: source service behind an edge.
ETag: representation validator.
Cache key: identity used to select a stored response.
lesson.safety: Use synthetic responses only. Do not invalidate production distributions or cache real credentials, cookies or profile data.
cleanup: Retain the fictional cache-policy matrix; no edge resources or public assets were created.
lesson.interview_question: A hypothetical CDN improves latency but users sometimes see another user's profile. What would you investigate immediately?
interview_points: Contain shared caching of personalized responses.
Inspect cache keys, variation and authorization handling.
Invalidate affected content through incident procedures.
Separate static asset policy from private response policy.

networking/cdns-caching-and-edge-deliver.core: Cache correctness depends on eligibility, key variation and freshness. No-cache requires validation; no-store prohibits storage. Separate personalized responses from public assets, and calculate origin load when hit ratios change.
objectives: Calculate miss traffic from hit ratio.
Design safe cache keys and freshness policies.
prerequisites: Understand HTTP headers, responses and origins.

storyboard.title: A path-only cache key confuses two users
storyboard.objective: Explain why cache variation is a data boundary.

scenes.title: The first response is stored
scenes.caption: A key containing only the path omits user identity.
scenes.narration: The edge fetches one user's profile and stores it under a path-only key, despite the representation being personalized.

scenes.title: Incorrect shared hit
scenes.caption: A second user matches the same cache entry.
scenes.narration: Another user requests the same path. The cache reuses the first profile because its key does not express the response's privacy boundary.

scenes.title: Contain and correct policy
scenes.caption: Do not share sensitive personalized responses.
scenes.narration: The operator disables inappropriate shared storage, follows invalidation procedures and verifies that public assets and private profiles have separate policies.
